title: Private Books: Jung's Black Books and Dick's Exegesis
subtitle: C. G. Jung in Zürich, 1912–1917, and Philip K. Dick in Fullerton, 1974 — with the long road to publication
intro: This chapter sets two private books on one timeline. Between 1913 and 1917 the Swiss psychiatrist C. G. Jung, newly cut off from Freud, recorded a long run of waking visions and inner dialogues in small black notebooks, then rewrote them as an illuminated manuscript he called Liber Novus. Sixty years later, in February and March 1974, the American novelist Philip K. Dick had a cluster of experiences he named '2-3-74' and spent the rest of his life writing about them in an enormous private notebook he called the Exegesis.

The two men did not share a century, a language or a profession, and their experiences are not offered here as the same. What they share is a pattern. Each was a professional builder of interpretations who suddenly had an experience he could not interpret. Each wrote it down at once, kept the full record close for the rest of his life, and let out only fragments: Jung a privately printed pamphlet and a small club, Dick long letters to a graduate student and fellow writers. Each book was opened to outside checking only decades after its author's death, in 2009 and 2011.

The record is honest only about one side. Jung's dated journals survive and are now published; the people he is said to have confided in, Toni Wolff and Maria Moltzer, left no published firsthand account of these years, and his wife Emma's surviving letters on the subject date from 1911. Dick's letters survive, but the replies of his main correspondents are unpublished, and his wife Tessa's recollections came decades later. Where a person appears here only through someone else's pages, the entry says so.

Much of the best-known material is later firsthand. The vision of a flood over Europe is told in Jung's memoir of 1962, written with Aniela Jaffé, and his reading of it as a forecast of the 1914 war is his own later interpretation. The fish sign at Dick's door is told in a speech of 1977 and an essay of 1978, and even its day is disputed. The record ledger at the end of the chapter measures the distance between each event and its first telling.

There is also a darker kind of checking. The same Dick who wrote patient letters about dreams wrote to the FBI naming fellow writers and critics as part of hidden schemes. A private world tested against others can become a private world imposed on them. All texts in this chapter are in copyright, so every entry is a summary in plain words, with links to the editions and archives.
calendar_note: All dates are Gregorian. The chapter has two time-blocks, 1911–1917 (Jung) and 1972–1978 (Dick), joined by later publications (1962, 2009, 2011, 2020); convergences mark parallel moments in the pattern as well as shared dates.
seam: Both records begin as notebooks no one else was meant to read and end, decades later, as edited books that others can date and dispute. In between, each man checked his strange idea against a few chosen people, and the entries show how narrow and one-sided that checking was: replies lost or unpublished, a wife who remembers a different object, colleagues named to the FBI without knowing. Like the private realities of The Lathe of Heaven, the inner world shaped how its owner read the outer one, from a war to a pharmacy delivery. The ledger keeps the gap between what was written that night and what was told years later.

eyes.name: Carl Gustav Jung
eyes.role: Swiss psychiatrist, aged 37–42; president of the International Psychoanalytical Association until April 1914; private practice at Küsnacht on Lake Zürich
eyes.side: Zürich school of analytical psychology, breaking from Freud's Vienna circle
eyes.where: Küsnacht, Zürich; travelling to Munich (1913) and Aberdeen (1914); military service at Château-d'Oex (1917)
eyes.vantage_label: the dreamer and keeper of the private books
eyes.form: dated private journals (Black Books), a calligraphic manuscript (Liber Novus), dated letters, and a memoir written later
eyes.authenticity: The seven Black Books (12 November 1913 onward, with entries to at least 1932) are dated contemporaneous journals, published in facsimile and translation in 2020 (Philemon Foundation / W. W. Norton, ed. Sonu Shamdasani). Liber Novus, the 'Red Book', was worked up from them from late 1914 and kept by the family until its 2009 facsimile. Memories, Dreams, Reflections (1962) was assembled with Aniela Jaffé in his last years and is later firsthand; where it and the journals differ (for example on when the 1914 dreams came), the journals are the earlier witness. All texts are in copyright: digests only.
eyes.bio: Jung broke with Freud in January 1913 and, by his own later account, spent the following years deliberately provoking and recording waking fantasies he feared might be psychosis. He wrote them in small black notebooks, rewrote them in a large illuminated volume, and showed them to almost no one. What he tested against others was not the visions themselves but the method and theory he drew out of them, in papers, lectures and a small club.

sources.title: Black Books (Jung) — overview of the seven journals and the 2020 edition
Lance Owens, History and the Transformation of Jung
Philemon Foundation introduction (Shamdasani)

eyes.name: Sigmund Freud
eyes.role: Viennese founder of psychoanalysis, aged 56–58; Jung's former mentor, who had once seen him as his successor
eyes.vantage_label: the friend who ended it, by letter
eyes.form: dated letters; a polemical history written soon after
eyes.authenticity: The Freud–Jung correspondence (1906–1913) was published in 1974 (ed. William McGuire), German and English. Freud's letter of 3 January 1913 is held in the Library of Congress Freud collection and was displayed in its exhibition. Modern translations are in copyright: digests only.
eyes.bio: Freud is the outside eye at the start of the story: the one person against whom Jung had tested every idea for six years. His letters show the break from the other side, and his 1914 history of the movement records how the Vienna circle read Jung's turn.

sources.title: Library of Congress, page from Freud's letter to Jung (1913)
Open Culture: the letter in which Freud breaks with Jung

eyes.name: Emma Jung (née Rauschenbach)
eyes.role: Jung's wife, mother of five, later an analyst in her own right; aged 30–35. No surviving firsthand account found of the 1913–1917 'confrontation' itself.
eyes.side: Jung household, Küsnacht; later Psychological Club member
eyes.vantage_label: in the same house, largely silent in the record
eyes.form: dated letters (1911, to Freud); otherwise no published record for 1913–17
eyes.authenticity: Her letters of autumn 1911 to Freud are printed in the 1974 Freud/Jung Letters. No diary or letter by her describing Jung's visions of 1913–1917 has been published; her own presence in those years is known mainly from Jung's journals and later biographers.
eyes.bio: Emma Jung wrote to Freud behind her husband's back in late 1911, worried that the friendship was cooling and that Jung's new book was pulling him away. For the years of the Black Books she is a missing voice: present in the house, absent from the published record.

sources.title: The Freud/Jung Letters (1974), overview

eyes.name: Antonia (Toni) Wolff
eyes.role: No surviving firsthand account found. Former patient of Jung, then his collaborator and intimate companion; aged 25–29; later an analyst and president of the Psychological Club
eyes.form: none published for these years; appears in Jung's journals and society minutes
eyes.authenticity: Wolff's own diaries and letters for 1913–1917 have not been published, and much of her correspondence with Jung is reported to have been destroyed. She appears in Jung's Black Books (an entry of 15 November 1913 is read by commentators as referring to her) and in the membership record of the Zürich society.
eyes.bio: Wolff is widely described as the person with whom Jung shared the fantasies as they came. If so, she was the first and closest 'check' on the private book, and she left almost nothing in her own words about it.

sources.title: Black Books study page (dated chronology, with footnotes)

eyes.name: Maria Moltzer
eyes.role: No surviving firsthand account found. Dutch nurse turned analyst, Jung's assistant in Zürich; aged about 39–44
eyes.vantage_label: colleague who argued back, in a lost letter
eyes.form: none surviving for these years; known from Jung's journals and recollections
eyes.authenticity: Moltzer's letters to Jung on his fantasies have not survived. Commentators identify her as the woman whose voice in Memories, Dreams, Reflections insists the fantasies are 'art', a reading Jung rejected; that identification is an inference, not a documented fact.
eyes.bio: Moltzer stands for the dissenting reader. According to Jung's own recollection, she pressed him to treat his fantasies as artistic work; he refused, insisting they were nature, not art. The argument survives only on his side.

sources.title: Black Books study page (Moltzer chronology)

eyes.name: Sonu Shamdasani
eyes.role: Historian of psychology (University College London); editor of Liber Novus (2009) and The Black Books (2020) for the Philemon Foundation
eyes.vantage_label: the editor who opened the books, a century on
eyes.authenticity: A modern scholarly witness to the documents, not to the events. Included because the chapter's subject is the slow checking of a private book against others.
eyes.bio: Shamdasani worked for over a decade with the Jung family's archive to transcribe, translate and date the Red Book and the Black Books. His editions turned a privately guarded manuscript into a checkable record with dates.

sources.title: Philemon Foundation introduction
Lance Owens on the 2009 publication

eyes.name: Philip Kindred Dick
eyes.role: American science-fiction novelist, aged 45 in 1974; living in Fullerton, Orange County, California, with his wife Tessa and their infant son Christopher
eyes.vantage_label: the experiencer and keeper of the private book
eyes.form: dated letters, an undated-to-dated private notebook (the Exegesis), and later speeches and essays
eyes.authenticity: The 1974 letters are printed in The Selected Letters of Philip K. Dick: 1974 (Underwood-Miller, 1991). The Exegesis is roughly eight thousand pages of handwritten and typed notes from 1974 to 1982; a selection was published by Houghton Mifflin Harcourt on 8 November 2011 (ed. Pamela Jackson and Jonathan Lethem). The Metz speech (1977) and the essay 'How to Build a Universe' (1978) are later firsthand. The novel VALIS (1981) is fiction and is used here only as context. All in copyright: digests only.
eyes.bio: In February and March 1974 Dick experienced what he came to call '2-3-74': a flash of recognition at a fish sign, then visions, voices and a sense of a hidden first-century reality under the present. He spent the remaining eight years writing theories about it, mostly for himself, while testing pieces of it in letters to a graduate student, to fellow writers, and, more darkly, to the FBI.

sources.title: Selected Letters 1974 (bibliographic record)
HMH press release on the Exegesis (2011)
Erik Davis, Philip K. Dick's Divine Interference

eyes.name: Claudia Krenz Bush
eyes.role: No published firsthand account found. Graduate student at Idaho State University writing a master's thesis on Dick; his most frequent correspondent on 2-3-74 in 1974–75
eyes.vantage_label: the distant reader he thought aloud to
eyes.form: recipient of dated letters; her replies are not published
eyes.authenticity: Dick's letters to her survive and many are included in the Exegesis edition (Folder 4). Her own replies have not been published.
eyes.bio: Bush mattered because she was outside Dick's household and his genre: a careful academic reader to whom he could send long, theory-laden letters. In them he works his experiences out on paper and sometimes cautions her, and himself, about trusting dreams.

sources.title: Letter to Claudia Bush, 5 July 1974 (summary page)
Letter to Claudia Bush, 29 November 1974 (summary page)

eyes.name: Tessa B. Dick (née Leslie Busby)
eyes.role: Dick's fifth wife, aged about 19–20 in 1974; mother of Christopher; present in the Fullerton apartment
eyes.vantage_label: in the room, telling it decades later
eyes.authenticity: Her accounts were given long after 1974 and are labelled later; on Dick's inner experience they are necessarily secondhand. One detail, that the gleam came from a fish sticker rather than a pendant, is known here as reported by the researcher Sarill on a Dick studies blog.
eyes.bio: Tessa Dick was the only other adult in the household. Her later recollections both support and complicate the familiar story: she places the day differently and remembers different objects.

sources.title: 'So when the heck is 2-3-74?' (dating discussion)

eyes.name: Thomas M. Disch
eyes.role: No firsthand account from 1972–74 found. American science-fiction novelist and critic, author of Camp Concentration (1968); a friend and admirer of Dick
eyes.vantage_label: named in a letter he never saw
eyes.form: none for these years; appears in Dick's letter to the FBI
eyes.authenticity: Disch was unaware at the time that Dick had named his novel to the FBI. His later reaction is known from his last novel and from secondary reports.
eyes.bio: Disch is the cost of the hidden world. Dick's suspicion that coded messages lay in Disch's novel shows the private theory spilling onto a real colleague without that colleague's knowledge.

sources.title: Black Gate, When Philip K. Dick reports you to the FBI

eyes.name: Ursula K. Le Guin
eyes.role: No published reply found. American novelist (The Lathe of Heaven, 1971); one of Dick's correspondents in the 1970s
eyes.authenticity: A Dick letter to Le Guin is printed in Selected Letters: 1974 (p. 247 per a Dick studies blog). Her side of the exchange has not been published.
eyes.bio: Le Guin represents the peer check: a fellow novelist of altered realities to whom Dick reported his February surgery and convalescence.

sources.title: Selected Letters 1974 (bibliographic record)
Dating discussion citing the Le Guin letter

eyes.name: Jonathan Lethem (with Pamela Jackson)
eyes.role: American novelist; co-editor, with Pamela Jackson, of The Exegesis of Philip K. Dick (2011)
eyes.vantage_label: the editors who opened the notebook
eyes.authenticity: A modern witness to the documents, not the events. Included because the chapter follows how the private book was finally checked by others.
eyes.bio: Lethem and Jackson led a team that sifted the Exegesis folders and published a selection with annotations nearly thirty years after Dick's death, turning a private, recursive notebook into a public text.

sources.title: Library of America blog: Lethem on the Exegesis (Nov 2011)
LA Review of Books, The Exegete

entries.headline: A wife writes to Freud behind her husband's back
entries.digest: Emma Jung wrote several letters to Freud in the autumn of 1911, uneasy that the friendship between the two men was cooling and anxious about how Freud would receive Jung's new book on the transformations of the libido. She asked Freud not to tell Jung she had written. They are the only letters in her own voice from the run-up to the break.
entries.source_note: Freud/Jung Letters (1974), Emma Jung's letters of Oct–Nov 1911; exact days not checked here.

entries.headline: A dream of a dove that became a girl
entries.digest: Shortly after Christmas 1912 Jung dreamed of a loggia, a dove that turned into a little girl, and a sense of being addressed by the dead. Writing decades later, he called this the point at which he became convinced the unconscious was alive in its own right. The dream is known from his later memoir, not a dated note of that night.
entries.source_note: Memories, Dreams, Reflections (1962), as summarised in the Black Books study chronology.

entries.headline: Jung tells Freud he treats pupils like patients
entries.digest: In a sharp letter Jung accused Freud of using analysis as a weapon, turning his followers into patients so as to stay above them. It was the letter that made a break unavoidable.
entries.source_note: Freud/Jung Letters (1974); date as commonly cited, not re-checked against the edition here.

entries.headline: Freud proposes ending all personal relations
entries.digest: Freud answered that a man who insists he is normal while behaving abnormally cannot be reasoned with, and proposed that they drop their private friendship altogether while keeping professional ties. He added that he would lose nothing by it. A page of this letter is held and displayed by the Library of Congress.
entries.source_note: Freud/Jung Letters; LoC exhibition page; Stadlen blog summary.

entries.headline: Jung accepts, and closes the door
entries.digest: Jung replied briefly that he would accede to Freud's wish, since he never forced his friendship on anyone, and that Freud himself knew best what the moment meant to him. He ended with Hamlet's last words. The private dialogue that had shaped him for six years was over.
entries.source_note: Freud/Jung Letters (1974); summary in Stadlen blog and Open Culture.

entries.headline: At Munich, a paper on types and a frosty congress
entries.digest: At the International Psychoanalytic Congress in Munich, Jung, still its president, spoke on two psychological attitudes, the turn outward and the turn inward. The Freudians present treated the meeting as a confrontation. It was his last public appearance as Freud's heir.
entries.source_note: Congress dates in the Black Books study chronology.

entries.place: On a journey (later accounts: by train, towards Schaffhausen)
entries.headline: A waking vision of Europe under a flood
entries.digest: Travelling alone, Jung later said, he was overtaken by an hour-long waking vision of a monstrous flood covering the low lands of northern Europe between the North Sea and the Alps, with the mountains rising to shield Switzerland, and rubble and drowned bodies in the water. He feared it meant his own mind was breaking. The account comes from his memoir and the Red Book, both written afterwards.
entries.source_note: Memories, Dreams, Reflections (1962); Liber Novus; summarised by the Jungian Center and the Black Books chronology.

entries.headline: The flood returns, redder
entries.digest: About a fortnight later, by his later account, the same vision came again, more vivid and with the water turned to blood, and an inner voice told him it was real and would happen. He did not read it as political: he read it as a threat of psychosis.
entries.source_note: Memories, Dreams, Reflections (1962), as summarised by the Jungian Center.

entries.headline: Jung resigns as editor of Freud's yearbook
entries.digest: Jung wrote to Freud giving up the editorship of the psychoanalytic yearbook, citing reports that Freud doubted his good faith. It is the last letter of their published correspondence.
entries.source_note: Freud/Jung Letters (1974); date as commonly cited, not re-checked here.

entries.headline: The first black notebook: calling for his soul
entries.digest: Jung opened the second of his small black notebooks with an appeal to his soul, asking where she had gone and saying he had come back to her after long wandering in the world. He resolves to stay with her and travel on together. It is the first dated page of the private record that would become the Red Book.
entries.source_note: The Black Books of C. G. Jung (2020), Book 2; Diaries of Note excerpt page; Wikipedia overview.

entries.headline: A woman whose soul mattered more
entries.digest: In an entry three days later, Jung's journal speaks of a woman whose soul meant more to him than his worries about his marriage. Commentators read this as Toni Wolff. It is her first appearance in the private book, and in Jung's words, not hers.
entries.source_note: Black Books 2, entry of 15 Nov 1913, as read in the Black Books study chronology.

entries.headline: Letting himself drop: the descent and the first figures
entries.digest: In mid-December Jung moved from watching his fantasies to entering them, imagining a descent and then conversing with figures he named, among them an old prophet and a blind young woman. He later called this period his most difficult experiment. Each night's dialogue was written up in the notebook, often with the date.
entries.source_note: Black Books, Dec 1913; Black Books study chronology; Lance Owens.

entries.headline: Moltzer and Wolff join the Zürich society
entries.digest: Maria Moltzer and Toni Wolff were admitted as lay members of the Zürich psychoanalytical society. The private visions were being written in Küsnacht; the circle that would test the ideas drawn from them was forming in Zürich.
entries.source_note: Society record as cited in the Black Books study chronology.

entries.date_display: Freud's history of the movement, early 1914
entries.headline: Freud writes the split into history
entries.digest: Within a year of the break Freud wrote a polemical history of the psychoanalytic movement, published in 1914, explaining why the Zürich and Adlerian departures were not psychoanalysis. It is the outside view of what Jung was doing, written without knowledge of the notebooks.
entries.source_note: Freud, 'On the History of the Psycho-Analytic Movement' (1914); month of writing not checked here.

entries.headline: Jung resigns as president of the International Association
entries.digest: Jung gave up the presidency of the International Psychoanalytical Association, completing his public withdrawal from Freud's movement. In July the Zürich group voted to leave it.
entries.source_note: Black Books study chronology (resignation 20 Apr; Zürich vote 10 Jul 1914).

entries.headline: Three dreams of killing frost
entries.digest: Jung dreamed three times that a wave of Arctic cold descended in midsummer and froze the land. His memoir places the three dreams in spring 1914; the dated journals and later scholarship place them in June and July. The gap between the two tellings is itself a lesson in how memory files things.
entries.source_note: Memories, Dreams, Reflections (spring); Black Books study chronology (June–July 1914).

entries.headline: In Aberdeen, a lecture on the unconscious
entries.digest: Jung lectured to the British Medical Association in Aberdeen on the importance of the unconscious in psychopathology. He was abroad as Europe slid into war, and later said he heard of the outbreak there.
entries.source_note: Black Books study chronology, fn. 113 (lecture date).

entries.headline: War: Jung's later reading of his visions
entries.digest: Germany declared war on Russia on 1 August. Jung later wrote that the outbreak relieved his fear of madness, because he now understood the flood and the frost as forebodings of the collective catastrophe. That reading is his interpretation, made after the fact; the 1913 notebook pages do not name a war. He later told an interviewer he learned the news on 31 July.
entries.source_note: War date: historical record. Interpretation: Memories, Dreams, Reflections; Black Books study chronology fn. 114–115.

entries.headline: The first draft of the new book is done
entries.digest: After a pause in the journals from June 1914, Jung compiled a typed draft from the notebooks, adding commentary; by August 1915 the first draft of Liber Novus was complete. He began copying it into a large leather volume in Gothic script with his own paintings, work he would continue on and off for sixteen years.
entries.source_note: Black Books (Jung) overview: hiatus June 1914 – late summer 1915; first draft by Aug 1915; Lance Owens on 16 years of calligraphy.

entries.headline: Seven Sermons, printed for friends only
entries.digest: Jung wrote a set of seven gnostic 'sermons to the dead', attributed to the ancient teacher Basilides, and had them privately printed in 1916. He gave copies only as gifts to friends and pupils. It was the one fragment of the Red Book he let out, without his name as author.
entries.source_note: Seven Sermons to the Dead (encyclopedia mirror): privately printed 1916, gifts only; reprinted in the 1962 German edition of the memoir.

entries.headline: A cosmogony in the notebook, and a first mandala
entries.digest: A journal entry records his soul presenting a whole cosmogony. Jung painted it as a diagram of the entire world, which he later called his first mandala. The private book was beginning to produce diagrams that could be shown and discussed.
entries.source_note: Black Books study chronology, fn. 144–145.

entries.headline: A club to test the ideas on others
entries.digest: The Psychological Club was founded in Zürich, funded by a large gift from Edith Rockefeller McCormick, with around sixty members at the start. It gave Jung a closed but real forum where the concepts emerging from his notebooks could be argued over.
entries.source_note: Black Books study chronology, fn. 136 (funding, membership); exact founding day not confirmed.

entries.headline: 'It is art': the colleague who disagreed
entries.digest: Jung later recalled a woman's voice, and a letter from a female colleague, insisting that his fantasies had artistic value. He answered that they were nature, not art. Commentators identify the colleague as Maria Moltzer; her letter does not survive, so only his side is known.
entries.source_note: Memories, Dreams, Reflections; Black Books study chronology (identification and dating are inference).

entries.headline: Daily circles in an army notebook
entries.digest: On military service at Château-d'Oex, Jung began sketching a small circular drawing each morning in his army notebook, using them to track his inner state. The mandalas became one of the few parts of the private work he later taught openly.
entries.source_note: Black Books study chronology (service 11 June – 2 Oct 1917; daily mandalas from 20 Aug).

entries.headline: Jung dies; the Red Book stays shut
entries.digest: Jung died at Küsnacht aged 85. The calligraphic volume, unfinished since about 1930, remained with his heirs, who kept it from publication for nearly fifty years.
entries.source_note: Standard biographical date; Liber Novus publication history (Lance Owens).

entries.headline: The memoir tells the visions for the first time
entries.digest: Memories, Dreams, Reflections, compiled from conversations with Aniela Jaffé and chapters Jung wrote himself in his last years, gave the public its first account of the 1913 flood vision, the 1914 dreams and the Seven Sermons. It is a firsthand telling from four decades later, shaped by an old man's sense of his life.
entries.source_note: Publication 1962; Seven Sermons included as appendix (Seven Sermons page).

entries.place: Fullerton (Dick's letter); Disch in New York
entries.headline: Dick names a colleague's novel to the FBI
entries.digest: Dick wrote to the FBI that a covert group had pressed him to hide coded information in his books, and that he had just found Thomas Disch's Camp Concentration, which he suspected contained such material. Disch knew nothing of it. It is the darker form of 'checking with others': a private theory reported to the state.
entries.source_note: Letter of 28 Oct 1972 quoted in Black Gate (citing Fortean Times on the FBI file).

entries.headline: A pink light and a hidden hernia
entries.digest: Dick later said that while a Beatles song played, a beam of pink light told him that his baby son had an undiagnosed birth defect. He and Tessa took the boy to a doctor, who found an inguinal hernia needing surgery. It is the episode he cited most often as evidence that the information was real, but no contemporary medical or diary record is published, and the date is not fixed.
entries.source_note: Erik Davis, Divine Interference; Exegesis; no dated contemporary record traced.

entries.headline: A new novel out, a tooth out
entries.digest: Doubleday published Flow My Tears, the Policeman Said in February 1974. Dick later wrote that the following week he had impacted wisdom teeth removed under sodium pentothal and went home in pain to recover.
entries.source_note: 'How to Build a Universe' (1978); Erik Davis, Divine Interference.

entries.date_display: 20 February 1974 (Sutin's date; others argue 14 or 21 February)
entries.headline: The fish sign at the door
entries.digest: A young woman delivering painkillers from the pharmacy came to the door wearing a small gold fish, which she said was a sign used by early Christians. Dick later wrote that the sight made him remember, in a flash, being a secret Christian in the first century. The day is uncertain: the biographer Sutin gives 20 February, but his notes do not support it, and other researchers reconstruct a Thursday, 14 or 21 February, between 4 and 5 in the afternoon.
entries.source_note: Dating discussion (Sutin p. 210; Sarill and Tessa Dick's reconstruction); 'How to Build a Universe' (1978).

entries.headline: What Tessa remembers: a sticker, not a pendant
entries.digest: As reported by the researcher Sarill, Tessa Dick said that the gleam came from sunlight on a reflective Christian fish sticker, not from a necklace. Her memory and her husband's diverge on the very object at the centre of the story. Her account is decades later and secondhand on his inner experience.
entries.source_note: Sarill's comment, reported in 'So when the heck is 2-3-74?' (2024).

entries.headline: Nights of colour and a landscape recognised
entries.digest: In March came the main run of experiences: nights of rapidly shifting abstract images, dreams, a sense of an intelligence speaking to him, and an overlay of an ancient Roman world on Orange County. He later said that in March 1974 he understood why a certain bleak landscape had haunted his fiction.
entries.source_note: Metz speech (1977) as summarised by Open Culture; Erik Davis, Divine Interference. Dick used '2-3-74' for February–March, not one day (Rickman, via dating blog).

entries.headline: Reporting the surgery to a fellow novelist
entries.digest: In a letter to Ursula K. Le Guin printed in the 1974 volume of his letters, Dick mentioned the major oral surgery he had undergone in February and his convalescence at home. Le Guin's reply is not published.
entries.source_note: Selected Letters 1974, p. 247, as cited in the dating blog (the blog's year label is inconsistent).

entries.headline: A dream of a blue book, and a warning about dreams
entries.digest: Dick told Claudia Bush of a dream that seemed to point him to a blue hardbound book with a title ending in 'Grove'. He found a match on his own shelves: a biography of Warren Harding, which he called the dullest book imaginable. In a postscript he told her not to put much faith in dreams.
entries.source_note: Letter to Claudia Bush, 5 July 1974 (Exegesis, Folder 4; summary page).

entries.headline: Lem, the critics and a 'committee'
entries.digest: Dick sent the FBI the letterhead of the critic Darko Suvin and named Suvin, Peter Fitting, Fredric Jameson and Franz Rottensteiner as Marxists linked to Stanisław Lem, whom he suggested was a committee rather than a single writer, gaining influence over science-fiction criticism and awards. None of those named knew. It is the private theory turned outward as suspicion.
entries.source_note: Letter of 2 Sept 1974 reproduced on Torn Branches; Culture.pl article.

entries.headline: Ubik as an immanent mind
entries.digest: Writing to Bush about Ubik and the screenplay he was drafting from it, Dick connected the novel's mysterious force to an 'immanent mind', a universal intelligence of which each person carries a fragment that can be awakened from outside. His own fiction had become evidence in his theory.
entries.source_note: Letter to Claudia Bush, 29 Nov 1974 (Exegesis, Folder 4; summary page).

entries.headline: At Metz: other worlds, overlapping
entries.digest: At a science-fiction festival in Metz, Dick told a French audience that time could be orthogonal, that many alternate presents overlap, and that a hidden programmer adjusts the variables while memories of discarded worlds sometimes leak through. He offered his own experiences, and his novel Flow My Tears, as a remembered alternate world. The audience, by most accounts, was baffled.
entries.source_note: Open Culture and Wikipedia pages on the speech; exact day not confirmed in fetched sources.

entries.headline: How to build a universe: the Acts parallel
entries.digest: In a talk written in 1978 and printed in 1985, Dick told the fish-sign story and said a priest had shown him that a scene in Flow My Tears matched one in the Acts of the Apostles, down to the names Felix, Jason and Philip, though he said he had never read Acts. He argued that the real setting was first-century Judaea, with the modern world a veil over it.
entries.source_note: 'How to Build a Universe That Doesn't Fall Apart Two Days Later' (1978; pub. 1985), text at philipdick.com and summary at aphelis.net.

entries.headline: Dick dies with the notebook unfinished
entries.digest: Dick died after strokes, aged 53. The Exegesis, by then thousands of pages in folders, was still being written and had never been prepared for print.
entries.source_note: Standard biographical date.

entries.headline: The Red Book is opened
entries.digest: Norton and the Philemon Foundation published a full-size facsimile and translation of Liber Novus, edited by Sonu Shamdasani, with its inaugural presentation on 8 October 2009. For the first time readers could compare the late memoir with the visions as Jung had written them up.
entries.source_note: Lance Owens page: published October 2009, inaugural presentation 8 Oct 2009.

entries.headline: The Exegesis in print
entries.digest: Houghton Mifflin Harcourt published a selection of the Exegesis edited by Pamela Jackson and Jonathan Lethem, with annotations by a team of readers. Lethem described it as a long, calamitous argument with the universe. Like Jung's book two years earlier, a private record was opened to checking only decades after its author's death.
entries.source_note: HMH press release (8 Nov 2011); Library of America blog, Nov 2011.

entries.headline: The black notebooks follow
entries.digest: The Black Books 1913–1932 appeared in seven volumes, in facsimile and translation, edited by Shamdasani. With their dates, the earliest layer of the private record could be set against both the Red Book and the memoir.
entries.source_note: Black Books (Jung) overview: 2020, Philemon Foundation / Norton.

convergences.label: The break, by letter (3–6 January 1913)
convergences.note: Freud proposes dropping the friendship; Jung accepts in a few lines. Emma Jung's letters of 1911 had already shown that someone inside the house saw it coming. The private dialogue ends, and the private notebook begins within the year.

convergences.label: The notebook opens (12–15 November 1913)
convergences.note: Jung's first entry calls for his soul; three days later the same notebook speaks of a woman who mattered more than his marital worries. Wolff, the person he is said to have confided in, is visible only through his pages.

convergences.label: The circle forms while the visions run (January–July 1914)
convergences.note: As Jung's journal fills with figures and dialogues, Moltzer and Wolff join the Zürich society and Jung leaves Freud's international association. Private record and public circle grow side by side.

convergences.label: War: the vision read backwards
convergences.note: Jung later read his 1913 flood as a forecast of the war; Freud, writing his history of the movement in 1914, saw only a doctrinal schism. Neither the notebook pages of 1913 nor Freud's essay mention the other's frame.

convergences.label: Letting a little out (1916)
convergences.note: The Psychological Club gives Jung a closed forum, and the Seven Sermons are printed for friends only. Moltzer, by Jung's later account, wanted the fantasies treated as art; he insisted they were nature. The test of the private book was social, but tightly limited.

convergences.label: The fish sign (February 1974)
convergences.note: Dick remembers a gold pendant and a flash of first-century memory; Tessa, decades later, remembers sunlight on a sticker and a different day. Two people in the same doorway leave two different objects.

convergences.label: Thinking aloud by post (1974)
convergences.note: Dick reports his surgery to Le Guin and works out dreams and theories in long letters to Claudia Bush, even warning her against trusting dreams. Their replies are not published, so the check is visible only from his side.

convergences.label: When checking becomes suspicion (1972–1974)
convergences.note: The same impulse that sent letters to a graduate student also sent letters to the FBI naming Disch's novel (1972) and Lem's critics (1974). Those named did not know they had been 'checked'.

convergences.label: The private books opened (2009 and 2011)
convergences.note: Liber Novus appears in October 2009, the Exegesis in November 2011, each decades after its author's death and each edited by outsiders who dated and annotated what had been kept close.

ties.note: Close collaborators and correspondents from 1906 until the break of January 1913.
Husband and wife; she lived through the 'confrontation' in the same house but left no published account of it.
She wrote to Freud privately in autumn 1911 about the strain between the two men.
Former patient, then collaborator and companion; commentators read her into the journal entry of 15 November 1913.
His assistant in Zürich; by his later account she argued his fantasies were art, and he rejected it.
Both admitted to the Zürich society on the same day in January 1914; Jung's notebooks are read as pairing them symbolically.
Edited, translated and dated Jung's Red Book (2009) and Black Books (2020).
Married in 1973; she was in the apartment in February 1974 and later gave her own differing recollections.
Dick's main 1974–75 correspondent on his experiences; his letters to her are part of the Exegesis.
Fellow novelist of altered realities to whom he wrote in 1974 about his surgery.
Friends in print, but Dick named Disch's novel to the FBI in 1972 without his knowledge.
Co-edited the Exegesis selection published in 2011.
Dick read Jung and drew on his ideas of archetypes and the collective unconscious in the Exegesis, though the two never met.

threads_out.note: Like the dreamers of that chapter, Jung told his visions fully only decades later, in a memoir; the gap between the dated notebook and the remembered night is the same gap that chapter's ledger measures.

Hildegard of Bingen also kept a visionary experience private for years before writing it down and seeking confirmation from authority; Jung and Dick each wrestled with the same question of whether a vision is revelation, art or illness.
Jung read his October 1913 flood vision and 1914 frost dreams as forebodings of the war that began on 1 August 1914, while he was lecturing in Aberdeen.
Freud's Vienna, where The Interpretation of Dreams appeared in 1899–1900, is the school Jung joined in 1906 and left in 1913.
Dick's 1977 Metz speech described overlapping alternate presents, a popular, non-technical echo of the many-worlds idea that physics had produced two decades earlier.
